lesson.title: Random Steps and Choices
lesson.driving_question: How can a program choose from a stepped sequence or a prepared collection?
lesson.primary_concept_family: Selecting stepped numbers and list items at random
lesson.concept_budget: Use randrange() for stepped whole numbers and choice() for one existing list item; no other random API is introduced.
misconceptions: The randrange() stop value is excluded.
choice() returns one existing list item.
A fixed seed controls the sequence during investigation.
lesson.progression_note: Completes the required Grade 7 random operations while reusing known list literals ahead of the full list strand.

shared_program.filename: Random Steps and Choices - Starter Code.py
shared_program.code:
import random
random.seed(4)
even_step = random.randrange(2, 13, 2)
colour = random.choice(["red", "blue", "gold"])
print("Move:", even_step)
print("Colour:", colour)

primm.prompt: Recall that range-style stop values are excluded and that a list literal stores several values in order.
List every possible even_step value. With seed 4, predict the exact number and colour before running the file.
Run twice unchanged, then remove the seed line and run several times. Check every number is even and every colour comes from the list.

questions: Why can random.randrange(2, 13, 2) produce 12 but not 13?
Why can random.choice() return only an item already present in its collection?
Why does using the same seed produce the same two results when the starter program is run again?
With seed 4, what two output lines appear?

primm.prompt: Generate a multiple of 5 from 5 through 30. Keep seed 4 and display the result as Move.
Add "green" to the colour choices and generate two independently stored colour selections. Display both selections on labelled lines.
Build a random training prompt. Choose an even repetition count from 2 through 12 and one activity from a three-item list you design. Display one instruction such as 8 jumps.
Repair the excluded stop value and pass the colour list into choice().
